<reason>B wins by exposing A's asymmetric comparison: A grants its preferred system effective regulation and durable subsidies while treating public-system funding failures as inevitable. B supplies concrete accountability mechanisms and shows why legal enrollment elsewhere does not establish affordability or uninterrupted treatment. A's concentrated-risk objection is meaningful, but its guarantees about provider continuity and annual public appropriations are unsupported. B more convincingly establishes employment-linked eligibility as an additional vulnerability without a demonstrated compensating advantage.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B directly attacks A's distinction between standing subsidies and annually appropriated public coverage: A never establishes that this funding asymmetry is inherent. A's final reply then demands protection from legislative changes, although B explicitly conceded that no system has such immunity.</best_rebuttal>
